blocks.html_en:
> The topic is "AI-generated images" in blog posts. Which, no, most of those aren't being generated with any of the more sophisticated techniques you're listing. And if they are, they're less likely to be the images people are complaining about and that are being discussed here.

The person you originally replied to scoped their comment to "decent usage", which to me implied some more process than just prompting.

> Does "synth" mean synthesized music?

Yes.

> A synthesizer is generally deterministic and the musician is making a decision about exactly what nodes are being played.

Generally but not always. There's plenty of synthetic music that leverage stochastic components. The stochasticity is a useful design constraint and is part of the artform. There's nothing that says art has to be deterministic or that the artist can't leverage nondeterminism in their artwork.

> Text prompt-based generation is a much higher level of abstraction which often makes several compositional and stylistic decisions for the user, even with advanced prompting.

There's also a whole genre of synthetic music called "Live Coding" which is typing programs to create synthetic music in front of an audience. There's also nothing that says art is only about making low level decisions.

> Go ahead and use AI-images in your blog post, I'm not gatekeeping or going to stop you. If they're so great, use a bunch of them everywhere. But, I (and people in this thread or that I know) will assume it's blogspam and click away.

It all depends on who you're looking to attract. The people I've met in AI focused communities have been awesome, always looking to experiment, try new things. The people against them I find very conservative and resistant to change (not saying this is you, or that it's necessarily bad). Which is fine if that's your audience, you have to know your readership. It's sort of like the difference between startup culture and enterprise culture. One is known for being nimble and innovative, the other for being reliable and capable. Positive signals to one are anti signals to the other. Threats like "I and people I know and the people in this thread won't frequent your blog" are met with shrugs, because that just means you're not the target audience.

blocks.html_en: > Does "synth" mean synthesized music?

sentences.en: > Does "synth" mean synthesized music?
sentences.zh: > “synth”是指合成音乐吗？

blocks.html_en: Yes.
> A synthesizer is generally deterministic and the musician is making a decision about exactly what nodes are being played.

sentences.en: > A synthesizer is generally deterministic and the musician is making a decision about exactly what nodes are being played.
sentences.zh: > 合成器通常是确定性的，音乐家正在决定到底播放哪些节点。

blocks.html_en: Generally but not always. There's plenty of synthetic music that leverage stochastic components. The stochasticity is a useful design constraint and is part of the artform. There's nothing that says art has to be deterministic or that the artist can't leverage nondeterminism in their artwork.

sentences.en: Generally but not always.
sentences.zh: 一般但并非总是如此。

sentences.en: There's plenty of synthetic music that leverage stochastic components.
sentences.zh: 有很多利用随机成分的合成音乐。

sentences.en: The stochasticity is a useful design constraint and is part of the artform.
sentences.zh: 随机性是一种有用的设计约束，也是艺术形式的一部分。

sentences.en: There's nothing that says art has to be deterministic or that the artist can't leverage nondeterminism in their artwork.
sentences.zh: 没有任何内容表明艺术必须是确定性的，或者艺术家不能在他们的艺术作品中利用非确定性。

blocks.html_en: > Text prompt-based generation is a much higher level of abstraction which often makes several compositional and stylistic decisions for the user, even with advanced prompting.

sentences.en: > Text prompt-based generation is a much higher level of abstraction which often makes several compositional and stylistic decisions for the user, even with advanced prompting.
sentences.zh: > 基于文本提示的生成是更高层次的抽象，即使有高级提示，它也经常为用户做出一些构图和风格决策。

blocks.html_en: There's also a whole genre of synthetic music called "Live Coding" which is typing programs to create synthetic music in front of an audience. There's also nothing that says art is only about making low level decisions.

blocks.html_en: It all depends on who you're looking to attract. The people I've met in AI focused communities have been awesome, always looking to experiment, try new things. The people against them I find very conservative and resistant to change (not saying this is you, or that it's necessarily bad). Which is fine if that's your audience, you have to know your readership. It's sort of like the difference between startup culture and enterprise culture. One is known for being nimble and innovative, the other for being reliable and capable. Positive signals to one are anti signals to the other. Threats like "I and people I know and the people in this thread won't frequent your blog" are met with shrugs, because that just means you're not the target audience.

blocks.html_en:
Indeed, including some AI generated things is becoming a costly signal that you're not bound by the neoluddites and the online anti-AI mob / redditor hivemind. I'm starting to like this signal, but it has to be distinguished from the simply being-lazy signal that indicates the content may not be all that interesting of valued by the author. If you have an otherwise high quality site where you aren't afraid to use AI for some elements, that makes me like it more.

It's a start of a barber's pole of fashion. Like when it became desirable to wear torn jeans even if you can afford proper ones. But you can only safely do it if you won't be confused with an actual hobo. It signals not playing by midwit pearl clutcher rules. So same with AI use. Don't play to the pearl clutchers, but don't be a hobo either. Shower but have somewhat torn jeans.

I mostly agree but here my analogy was reversed compared to yours. In my analogy the nicely dressed church lady is the professional, politically correct, climate conscious, anti AI redditor. The torn clothes punk hobo is the lazy rulebraking AI shoveler who makes the shared spaces dirty, and the smart iconoclast contrarian rebel artist poet ignoring schoolmarm rules is the person who uses AI but also makes otherwise high quality content.

(don't get hung up on the climate thing - I'm not arguing on the object level. A Christian believer can also be annoyed by the Karen-like peal clutcher no-fun-allowed church lady archetype).

Not that either are OK, but McDonalds basically stages their food to make it look more appealing, adding stuff that isn't in the product to make it look nicer.

https://youtu.be/pSYw8LTXXJM?is=FsJwTFKUkeDt1Z2Y

Tangentially, I kinda like the idea of Doordashs crowd sourced food images. Take a Pic of your food before you eat and get like a $5 discount if it is chosen. Customers are not likely to manipulate the product (they may stage it nicely like you mentioned but won't put browning agent or other additives to make it shinier).

blocks.html_en:
>> When I see pictures of food on a menu, I expect them to be real pictures of an example of the actual dish I'd get

> I don't get who would think that's a good idea.

It's super helpful to the customer, because it gives you a much better idea of what you're going to get. That's especially true with ethic food, where the descriptions use unfamiliar terms or a lot of meaning is lost in translation.

> Like if I order something because the picture shows that the dish has carrots or something and the dish you bring doesn't I'm going to complain.

Seriously, what's the problem with that?

Are you, for some strange reason, taking the perspective of a restaurant that wants to behave in a very customer-unfriendly way? Randomly dropping or substituting ingredients is not something a restaurant should be doing.

blocks.html_en: Last Christmas I caught our municipality (I'm from Greece) posting announcements about Christmas events on brochures that were choke full of obvious AI-generated images with Santa Claus, deer, trees, etc. and my first reaction was wondering exactly how hard would it have been if they were to hire artist(s) from our region, even if it was volunteer work, to have them promote their work instead. That's what a community is about.

sentences.en: Last Christmas I caught our municipality (I'm from Greece) posting announcements about Christmas events on brochures that were choke full of obvious AI-generated images with Santa Claus, deer, trees, etc. and my first reaction was wondering exactly how hard would it have been if they were to hire artist(s) from our region, even if it was volunteer work, to have them promote their work instead.
sentences.zh: 去年圣诞节，我发现我们的市政府（我来自希腊）在宣传册上张贴了有关圣诞节活动的公告，宣传册上充满了明显的人工智能生成的圣诞老人、鹿、树木等图像，我的第一反应是想知道，如果他们雇佣我们地区的艺术家，即使是志愿者工作，让他们宣传自己的作品，会有多困难。

sentences.zh: 这就是社区的意义所在。

Truth be told, they didn't put much effort into it before GenAI.

Those restaurants that use AI menus now? They just used free templates before. Few mom'n pop restaurants could afford spending money on graphic designers to work out a nice menu.

Usually they'd just use a template, send to the printer (or print it themselves), and that's what you got.

blocks.html_en:
> Are you speaking in the abstract, or would you, personally, like that when reading a blog?

It's better than the current status quo, where people post LLM writing without attributing it to the LLM, hoping you'll get tricked into reading.

At least if it's labeled like the GP describes, you know what you're getting and can make your own decision.

On the other hand:

> (It might also be the only way to stop training models on their own output)

On the other hand, I think it's a moral imperative to make it so the models train on their own output. I have absolutely no interest in giving them clean input data. After reading about how ISBNdb is helping them destroy old pre-LLM books for input, I totally think someone who does not have small children should start creating print-on-demand forgeries of such books (with the same ISBN numbers) filled with the most garbage-quality LLM text possible.

blocks.html_en:
I don't mind it for footnote/reference-book type material, where you want to have some information available for the curious but 99% of your readers won't care.

A few dense paragraphs about a database implementation that's ancillary to a story about the content of the database, for example; a small percentage of readers might want to reimplement or host A Thing locally and it could be helpful to know that it's this type of database with that number of tables and takes up x gigbytes on disk etc.

You are thinking of something nice to have. At least half the idea here is that it would be nice not to have something.

Usually there are many buttons and links one wouldn't click on.

If authors can't resist having chunks of copy paste slop in the middle of their article they can do it in a way I don't have to see it.

They also get a fair opportunity to impress me with a prompt that looks interesting enough.

And they get to distance themselves from the idea that copying [say] a Wikipedia article into a blog posting is the same as writing something.

blocks.html_en:
I just sat through my first fully AI-generated presentation. The content was as bland and straight down the middle as possible. The slides were all generated by a standard design - a mix of text blocks, bullets, fonts, colors.

Yeah, I have told people that I’m fully capable of typing things into ChatGPT or Claude myself. What I need from people are their own warty ideas. Sometimes real ideas are blurry or incomplete. Or have open questions. Making your own presentation can be a personal exercise in clarifying your thoughts. And sometimes the fact that ideas are half-baked or tricky is exactly why you’re having the meeting in the first place…

I guess if you’re in an environment where the emphasis is put on busy-work and formalities, then you’re going to get this sort of shit. Deeper organizational problem at that point, though…

blocks.html_en:
I’m inclined to agree, but not as much because the image was generated with AI but rather because it’s rare for such images to exhibit taste. They feel like the visual equivalent of gilded twinkies, which is offputting.

Selecting a stock image doesn’t have this effect, even if it’s not related to the post. Even the most unremarkable stock image has the fingerprints of its artist, and the choice itself can reveal things about the author. They don’t have that hyper-polished unintentioniality and subtle uncanny hollow “wrongness” that generated images do.

blocks.html_en: Taste is about matching things. If you stick Van Gogh's Starry Night into a blog post about profitmaxxing because you know it increases your discoverability by 0.02%, you have no taste. If you stick a pleasingly-proportioned image of a sailboat bobbing peacefully on a calm sea at sunset on a blog post about getting away from it all, it might be a perfect fit.

blocks.html_en:
This hasn’t been my wife’s experience at all. She manually writes all her content, but uses AI images as sizzlers for the scenes (fan fic for popular shows). Short of getting the actors together for a million bucks, she’d be hard pressed to make these scenes a reality. It’s also supposed to be aspirational, like “what if the tv cast got back together for another season hey?” I think the average person just doesn’t really notice.

Manually written content with an AI teaser image is perfectly acceptable to most people, including technical audiences who dislike AI writing.

There’s a very vocal minority who will get turned off by AI anything right now, even when it’s not part of the main content. Using AI for the main content is a no-no. The actual content that they came for has to show signs of authenticity.

blocks.html_en:
I'm fairly AI-pilled, as the cool kids say. But it would be fair for any AI-generated work to be labelled as such. The problem is, vast majority isn't doing it, because they know what the perception is like.

The question is, should we spend the same amount of time evaluating AI-gen work as non-AI-gen work. I would say no. In my opinion, AI-gen work should be evaluated by other AIs. Goes back to the whole "if you didn't put effort into creation, why should I put effort into evaluation" thing. Obviously it's not an all-or-nothing thing. But you get my point.

blocks.html_en:
It is all of those things and more.

Ethical: favour the notion that humans should be who we look to for writing, and that some of them are hopefully meaningfully compensated for it

Political: favour the decentralisation of effort away from US cloud AI firms

Practical: there's too much to read in the world; a very useful quality signal is to favour things obvious people put obvious effort into

Personal: it is soul-destroying that we live in a world that suddenly devalues people and their efforts so completely.

I think perhaps you are showing your own bias here. But abusing people for their chosen principles is not a business-winning strategy.

blocks.html_en:
> Plot twist, 100% likely you've read and shared humanized AI content.

I'm sure this has happened. If the author can speak with authority about everything that has written, then ya, I have to concede that is fine. It's obviously the most true when you are going to be engaging with the author. If you ask them a question and they respond, "I'm no sure, the LLM wrote it," that is a huge problem (and pretty pathetic, I might add).

> but if you were interested in subject of the article and its assertions and you nope out because of an AI writing tic, that's just toolish.

Meh, it I can find another article on the same subject written by a person then it's not too toolish. I've never liked this argument. It's the same thing with music. Even if I like a piece of music, and then I find out it's AI, I'm not going to listen to it. I can understand why people think this is stupid, but there is SO much music--even before it exponentially exploded with AI--that I can find something else I really like created by a person. Especially since when something really tickles my fancy, I like to read everything I can about the artist (which is an indirect form of engagement).

sentences.zh: 如果你问他们一个问题，他们回答说，“我不确定，法学硕士写的，”这是一个大问题（而且相当可悲，我可能会补充）。>但如果你对这篇文章的主题及其断言感兴趣，而你因为人工智能写作抽搐而放弃，那只是工具性的。嗯，如果我能找到另一篇由某人写的关于同一主题的文章，那么它就不算太工具性了。

blocks.html_en:
I don't agree, especially for this argument.

I'm a major AI user. Coding? Sure. But language learning, some art projects, TTRPG design. I'm so far 'lost' that I have a number of AI songs on my YouTube play list. For the anti-AI people, I'm like a walking abomination.

Yet despite all this, I still am a firm believer in "if you couldn't be bothered to write it, I can't be bothered to read it" as a default stance. I feel human to human communication should remain human to human. If AI is involved, the extent should be limited to where the human to human communication couldn't be achieved otherwise and fully disclosed.

Someone might even say I'm a bit of a hypocrite. Why do I like listening to an AI song but not reading an AI blog. Honestly, I'm not sure. I'm actually a bit puzzled by it myself. Regardless of the why, I think I should be an example of someone who holds this position for reasons entirely different than those you suggest.

I don't even disagree with you in general, a lot of AI discourse does seem to have bad faith arguments put forward and I do tire of some of them. But this specific one is one of the more few that seem good faith enough we should steelman it.

I have to believe that this is an attempt to be sensationalist, because I cannot possibly fathom someone actually believing this in good faith. blocks.html_en:
If they ask for my time, then they owe me theirs.

If you create something AI generated and post it in spaces where people expect to engage with other humans by way of human-created artifacts, then at best you’re dishonestly wasting everyone’s time. At worst, using AI generated responses to substitute for discourse assumes that other peoples’ time and attention are worth less than your own and direct communication is beneath you.

blocks.html_en: To cancel someone was really popular for a couple years starting just after covid. There's probably a better definition somewhere, but basically it is when a collective of like-minded people decide to publicly shame a person until they are too embarrassed to have an online presence, or even worse, until companies are pressured to not employ the person. It was like unofficial unions against someone existing. It stopped after enough people were cancelled that they were no longer powerless together. Then people who hate others had to evolve into different ways to be disrespectful because this method stopped working, which is why you don't see cancelling anymore

sentences.en: It was like unofficial unions against someone existing.
sentences.zh: 这就像针对现有存在的非正式工会。

sentences.en: It stopped after enough people were cancelled that they were no longer powerless together.
sentences.zh: 当足够多的人被取消后，他们不再一起无能为力，这种情况就停止了。

blocks.html_en: To cancel someone was really popular for a couple years starting just after covid. There's probably a better definition somewhere, but basically it is when a collective of like-minded people decide to publicly shame a person until they are too embarrassed to have an online presence, or even worse, until companies are pressured to not employ the person. It was like unofficial unions against someone existing. It stopped after enough people were cancelled that they were no longer powerless together. Then people who hate others had to evolve into different ways to be disrespectful because this method stopped working, which is why you don't see cancelling anymore

blocks.html_en:
I recently complained to the marketing team about an AI generated image used on our website main dashboard. I described everything that was wrong with the image the more you stared at it. That if I was a customer, I would feel that if they are ok to show a low quality image there, what does it means to the products I'm buying.

Their first reaction was to say they didn't see any problem with the image, then they changed it for an abstract image that I couldn't tell if it was AI or not, which is a huge improvement.

I thought I was alone in feeling this way, but turns out people from the sales team told me privately that they were happy I had spoken up.

sentences.zh: 我最近向营销团队抱怨我们网站主仪表板上使用人工智能生成的图像。

sentences.en: I described everything that was wrong with the image the more you stared at it.
sentences.zh: 当你盯着它看的越多时，我就会描述出图像中所有错误的地方。

sentences.zh: 如果我是客户，我会觉得如果他们可以在那里展示低质量的图像，这对我购买的产品意味着什么。他们的第一反应是说他们没有看到图像有任何问题，然后他们将其更改为抽象图像，我无法判断它是否是人工智能，这是一个巨大的进步。我以为我是唯一有这种感觉的人，但结果销售团队的人私下告诉我，他们很高兴我说出来了。

blocks.html_en:
Part of the problem is many bloggers think an image is required for every post. This is reinforced by algorithms which favor such posts, and drives bloggers to the easiest/fastest sources of free images.

The "featured image" in Wordpress is what gets shown on the index page, in shared social posts, and other contexts. And certainly, the algorithms favor such posts over pure text posts, even if the text content in the spartan post is far better.

There are other factors at play, too. Many bloggers are lazy, some are severely time constrained, a few are fearful of legal repercussions associated with copying images off the Internet, and a majority are creatively or technically incapable of making their own images to include on a personal blog post.

sentences.en: Part of the problem is many bloggers think an image is required for every post.
sentences.zh: 部分问题是许多博主认为每篇文章都需要一张图片。

sentences.en: This is reinforced by algorithms which favor such posts, and drives bloggers to the easiest/fastest sources of free images.The "featured image" in Wordpress is what gets shown on the index page, in shared social posts, and other contexts.
sentences.zh: 支持此类帖子的算法强化了这一点，并促使博主找到最简单/最快的免费图像来源。Wordpress 中的“特色图像”是在索引页面、共享社交帖子和其他上下文中显示的内容。

sentences.zh: 当然，与纯文本帖子相比，算法更喜欢此类帖子，即使斯巴达帖子中的文本内容要好得多。还有其他因素在起作用。

("radical" is a key word here -- there are numerous legitimate reasons to be critical of numerous aspects of the AI boom.)

I won't respond further.

I think you misunderstood what I said. Let me rephrase.

Would you rather watch a chess tournament between two of the best human players in world, or between two of the best bots in the world?

I know that chess is deeper than this, its about the positions that are reached and what each game adds to the existing knowledge and in that case it doesn't matter if its a human or bot. I understand very well that there is allot a Grandmaster can learn from games between two strong bots.

For my wife's birthday, I generated a fantastical image of our family (me, her, daughter, two cats) because staging such a thing IRL would have been difficult. It took me several hours to take some nice photos of my cats and daughter and then composite them and then generate an image i liked. Then I sent it to a framer and got it framed.

She loved it!

I think there's a time and a place for AI generated images that actually require care to generate a good result. I guess to use a cliché, its the thought that counts.

blocks.html_en:
It's pretty neat, actually. If you use Gemini's Nano Banana with a photo reference, it's pretty good at keeping most of the things that matter. I walk down 4th Street daily and that's pretty much what it looks like near Berry St.

And the thing I'm trying to remember is not, say, her athleisure or his white jacket. I'm trying to remember a couple with a dog with the man carrying a bag and a garbage grabber.

This notion of precision is actually an interesting thing to me. It's a question of what I'm trying to memorialize. Their clothes or their fitness or the colour of their dog doesn't matter so much.

You know, like some people object to statues of John Muir because he said some things like calling indigenous people "dirty and irregular" and stuff like that. But I think statues don't memorialize the man, they memorialize the symbolic man. The actual John Muir is dead, and we have his memetic descendant John Muir The Image. John Muir the image is a chalk drawing of John Muir the man, and the fact that the latter liked a dog, or hated boiled potatoes, or loved a woman, or whatever is irrelevant to me. I have taken this person, and flattened him on a canvas, and painted his acts on them as a guideline for myself. The rest of him is gone. And I like it that way.

I've had this as a draft post on the blog for a while so if you don't quite get what I'm saying about this accepted imprecision, it's probably because I haven't yet found a way to write this idea out in a clearer way.

blocks.html_en: Some content creators are too focussed on their work that they might not have noticed the debate going on online about AI-generated images and all they wanted was a cool image for their content. blocks.html_en:
It’s not about using new technology, it’s about the signal of effort.

Blind copy-pasting an AI image anywhere is a poor signal of effort, because it was a deliberate decision by the author… “I didn’t do the work to make this look professional, but my hope is that people THINK it looks professional.”

sentences.en: It’s not about using new technology, it’s about the signal of effort.Blind copy-pasting an AI image anywhere is a poor signal of effort, because it was a deliberate decision by the author…
sentences.zh: 这与使用新技术无关，而是关于努力的信号。盲目地将人工智能图像复制粘贴到任何地方都不是努力的信号，因为这是作者故意的决定......

sentences.en: “I didn’t do the work to make this look professional, but my hope is that people THINK it looks professional.”
sentences.zh: “我并没有做让这看起来很专业的工作，但我希望人们认为它看起来很专业。”

blocks.html_en:
If you're writing a personal blog (as opposed to a company blog), you should not care what people think.

A blog is an expression of your own taste. Write about things that interest you. Write in a style that you like. Add whatever images you want. And don't let some random stranger on the internet influence your blog. Otherwise, it's not your blog anymore.

sentences.en: If you're writing a personal blog (as opposed to a company blog), you should not care what people think.A blog is an expression of your own taste.
sentences.zh: 如果您正在撰写个人博客（而不是公司博客），您不应该关心人们的想法。博客是您自己品味的表达。

sentences.en: Write about things that interest you.
sentences.zh: 写一些你感兴趣的事情。

sentences.en: Write in a style that you like.
sentences.zh: 用你喜欢的风格来写。

sentences.en: Add whatever images you want.
sentences.zh: 添加您想要的任何图像。

sentences.en: And don't let some random stranger on the internet influence your blog.
sentences.zh: 并且不要让互联网上的一些随机陌生人影响您的博客。

sentences.en: Otherwise, it's not your blog anymore.
sentences.zh: 否则，它就不再是你的博客了。

I've recently started doing crude drawings on my reMarkable when needing something like explainer diagrams. It looks like a toddler did it, but, you know what? It works. I just stopped feeling weird about it.

blocks.html_en:
That may be your preference, but it's quite contrary to mine.

I have successfully used AI to generate generates "concept art" and logos for projects, presentations, and publications. It seems to make the outcomes more approachable, more understandable, and certainly more aesthetically pleasing.

It is not a matter of replacing human effort or skill, and certainly not a matter of adding cheap ornamentation. If AI weren't available, I usually wouldn't have the time, money, energy, or will to pursue those illustrations. I say this as someone who has historically spent what seems like a vast amount of time, energy, and money sourcing art. In a former life as as publisher I even hired full-time artists and insisted on custom artwork. But my current work no longer has that luxury. I still want the best possible looks, and the best possible outcomes.

blocks.html_en:
See other top HN article rn about "expertise is essential for using LLMs". Nobody is debating whether illustrators, graphic designers or marketers are going to use AI. In addition to being a thoroughly sailed ship, the sheer demand for constant content and image generation makes it a job skill at this point.

TFA is about blogs written by people with non-graphic expertise, who think it's great to, e.g., punctuate every other point with a way-too-detailed picture of a panda bear coder orchestrating fleets of squirrel agents. (Yes I'm looking at you Steve Yegge.) Nobody needs to be abused with this crap, and it all has the same overpolished overdetailed look, the "it's too good to be drawn by the author but is obviously NOT drawn by anybody with any visual sense".

It's not just blogs -- bands are now making these ridiculous "pro" fliers, food carts have stupid pictures of their owners on them -- but in blogs that ostensibly are written by humans for humans, AI images are worse than distracting and a very negative signal.

sentences.zh: 请参阅其他顶级 HN 文章，了解“专业知识对于使用法学硕士至关重要”。

sentences.en: Nobody is debating whether illustrators, graphic designers or marketers are going to use AI.
sentences.zh: 没有人争论插画师、图形设计师或营销人员是否会使用人工智能。

sentences.zh: 除了成为一艘彻底航行的船之外，对持续内容和图像生成的纯粹需求使其成为目前的一项工作技能。TFA 是由具有非图形专业知识的人撰写的博客，他们认为用一张过于详细的熊猫编码员编排松鼠代理舰队的图片来强调每一个点都是很棒的。

sentences.en: (Yes I'm looking at you Steve Yegge.)
sentences.zh: （是的，我正在看着你，史蒂夫·耶吉。）

blocks.html_en: Fair. The same is true of stock images and a lot of other visuals. Some writers just include images that are relevant, but a lot of them read some study indicating that imagery generated X% more page views and y% longer reading times and just developed the habit of sticking something on every post. If you think those studies are valid and are still inclined to do this, consider mining Wikipedia or some other site for obscure but interesting things and including a thoughtful caption, as well as a link to the full resolution image.

blocks.html_en:
I've developed an internal heuristic that tells me people who think an AI image to fill some blank space in any way improves anything aren't saying anything of value. There's a strong likelihood they're just trying to promote some product or scam. I came to this conclusion after seeing 100% of sites with AI images plastered on them being scams and BS with no actual value.

Meanwhile, a blog that's basic HTML and text and looks like it's fresh from 1998 is generally high quality info. People who are willing to write like that and publicly share it have confidence in what they're writing. And if that blog spreads, it's because the content is good. Not because it was eye catching at a glance.

sentences.zh: 他们很可能只是想推销某些产品或骗局。

How does your heuristic handle your qualitative and quantitative words here? If you land on a blog post with a single, pertinent illustration (from a LLM), do you assume the post, site and author are all robot trash and run away? Investigate the other posts before reading further?

The point of my caps, above was that I'm writing for me. If I think my post is improved by me prompting a LLM for an illustration, that's up to me. I'm not writing for your heuristic, I'm trying to express myself every way I can. The time where you find individuals untainted or unaided by these tools is over.

I'd try to just content by it's content rather than it's illustrations.

Most of the people that do this don’t have the basic human decency to start with a clear message like “All or some of this content is AI generated.”

blocks.html_en:
Just like published books were considered a symbol of effort that no one would have considered a blog as being anywhere near. When was the last time you looked up a book to find an answer to your question? That USED to be the normal.

Then we just googled for a link to Stack Overflow. And the oldtimers waxed lyrical on Slashdot, bemoaning the loss of craftsmanship, and how it was too easy nowadays - no effort.

What has been will be again, what has been done will be done again; there is nothing new under the sun.

The likely next normal will be agent-scraped content that it summarizes and tailors to its human. Slop, lacking real content, will be dutifully skipped by the agent, and the human won't care.

Meanwhile, armies of advertisers will cry foul, and scramble for a new way to get in front of human eyeballs.

And for those who want to continue reading blogs for pleasure, it's one agent pre-screen away.

Tempora mutantur, nos et mutamur in illis.

blocks.html_en:
Not all of us can afford to hire illustrators for every blog entry, and while an MS Paint squiggle might suit this blog's author's tastes, I can sympathize with anyone who might prefer something more sophisticated.

I don't see what the problem is with AI images, if some thought has been put into the image itself and if it's relevant in some way. I'd far rather see something playful and on-topic than the generic stock images littering blogs previously or some random example of the writer's photography with little connection to the article.

But really, whatever I like or don't like is besides the point. The blog using AI images isn't my blog. And if I was one of the blog authors who've sent this author into full prig-mode, I'd say to him, "No worries, Nelson. Have a happy life." I'd wager the blog author's own life wouldn't be any happier for bowing to the sensibilities of the Nelsons of this world.

sentences.en: Have a happy life."

sentences.zh: 我敢打赌，博客作者自己的生活不会因为屈服于这个世界的纳尔逊家族的情感而变得更幸福。

I think the issue is we all have read a bit into a AI article before realizing it is one and realize foolishly that you have been reading drivel.

The original prompts might have had something interesting to say, but it is so layered with filler and platitudes that it is just a waste.

After being burned enough times, we hunt around for signals that an article is about to waste our time.

Not all articles with AI images are LLM written, but almost all LLM written articles have AI images.

The author is telling you a hueristic is that people are using, and for this person here, I am totally doing it.

A picture of a napkin doodle at this point is superior.

It's a lie. It tricks the reader looking for deeper meaning.

Though hastily chosen non-AI images may do this too.

blocks.html_en:
I don't think the internet as we know it is going to survive generative AI.

Before, the simple existence of the content of some basic level of quality was a strong signal of effort, which corresponds strongly to value. If it's there, it's worth reading.

Now, the existence of content of a basic level of quality signals nothing. It might have some value, but it's much more likely it's useless AI slop.

This principle -- if it's there it's probably worth taking a look at -- undergirded so much of system of creation, discovery, and sharing that made the internet special -- blogs, open-source, posts, comments.

It allowed the gatekeepers, middlemen, guided channels, and tolls to be removed from the creation, enjoyment, sharing, and consumption of content.

I'm worried we're going to have to go back, just to get away from the avalanche of crap people are using AI to produce at crazy rate.

sentences.zh: 我不认为我们所知道的互联网能够在生成式人工智能中生存下来。以前，某些基本质量水平的内容的简单存在就是努力的强烈信号，这与价值密切相关。

sentences.zh: 如果存在，那就值得一读。现在，基本质量水平的内容的存在没有任何信号。

sentences.zh: 它可能有一些价值，但更有可能是无用的人工智能废话。这个原则——如果它存在的话，可能值得一看——巩固了使互联网变得特别的创造、发现和共享系统——博客、开源、帖子、评论。它允许把关人、中间人、引导渠道和收费从内容的创建、享受、共享和消费中删除。我担心我们将不得不去回来，只是为了摆脱人们使用人工智能以疯狂的速度生产的大量垃圾。

blocks.html_en:
Eh. I tend to use stock photo stuff. Even easier than AI (and most stockhouses are now using AI, themselves). If it's important to the story, I'll generally generate it, myself (I tend to use OmniGraffle a lot). I'm quite capable of making my own images.

The biggest thing, for me, is provenance. I sometimes get amazed at how people just grab any image they want, and slap it into their blog. There's a whole class of scammer, that goes around spamming fake "we're gonna sue you" letters to sites (I have gotten them, for images that I know are completely clear of obligation). If the image really was ripped off, then they won't be scammers, sending the emails.

I'd rather someone use an AI-generated image; especially if it's just "window dressing," than they put themselves into legal jeopardy, by pirating images.

blocks.html_en:
My my knee jerk reaction is to agree, I really hate the obvious looking AI images, though I suspect ultimately it comes down to having good taste.

blocks.html_en:
In the 80's, many, many people looked down on electronic and synthesized music because it wasn't real music played with real instruments.

And now it's just another instrument and has whole genres of music dedicated to it. C64 SID chips are sought after for 8-bit music creation because it has a unique aesthetic. Same with TR-808 drum machines.

The AI complaints feel a lot like that.

I'm betting in about 15-20 years there's going to be a revival of terrible AI images and videos because people are nostalgic for 2024 when AI images were obvious and sit firmly in an uncanny valley.

And I think AI will inspire a massive artistic revolution, both because it becomes just another tool in the toolbox that makes creation easier like drum machines and synths, AND it takes over the pop-music space previously occupied by boy bands and pop queens - generic rehashes of inoffensive crap that so saturates the market entire counter-cultures develop. But someone will use it to make something uniquely creative and new. Rap and hip-hop wouldn't exist without cheap drum machines.

In other words, you're old enough to start disliking new stuff, but not old enough to have seen this happen multiple times and realize that this is just another generational cycle. The younger generations will absorb AI tools and continue to do what humans have always done, which is be creative with the tools at their disposal.

blocks.html_en:
The main problem is, those AI generated images are only so jarring because they're so obvious.

As time goes on they'll be harder to spot. We're going to need a new way of determining quality as such obvious signals have a limited shelf-life.

Not that AI generated images are always bad. They are perfectly acceptable if used for (not an exclusive list): small separators between sections in large blog posts, or other decorative features; used to illustrate things for which no real image exists (as long as it's labelled as an impression/reconstruction/etc.). They're only really a negative signal if they're used dishonestly, to claim something existed when it didn't, etc.

sentences.zh: 我们需要一种新的方法来确定质量，因为这种明显的信号的保质期是有限的。并不是说人工智能生成的图像总是不好的。

sentences.zh: 如果用于（不是唯一的列表），它们是完全可以接受的：大型博客文章中各部分之间的小分隔符，或其他装饰功能；用于说明不存在真实图像的事物（只要它被标记为印象/重建/等）。

sentences.zh: 如果它们被不诚实地使用，声称某些东西存在但实际上并不存在，等等，它们实际上只是一个负面信号。

blocks.html_en:
Charles Baudelaire argued photography could not be considered a fine art because it merely produced mechanical replicas of reality without input from human imagination. He called photography "art's most mortal enemy" and the "refuge of all failed painters" who lacked artistic talent and training.

And if he's to be believed in 1859, photography isn't art.

But today, it's widely accepted that it is. And in all likelihood, you think it is too.

Why is that? And if you have an answer, you'd have to argue why AI generated images wouldn't follow the same trajectory.

sentences.zh: 查尔斯·波德莱尔认为摄影不能被视为一门美术，因为它只是产生现实的机械复制品，而没有人类想象力的输入。

sentences.en: He called photography "art's most mortal enemy" and the "refuge of all failed painters" who lacked artistic talent and training.And if he's to be believed in 1859, photography isn't art.But today, it's widely accepted that it is.
sentences.zh: 他称摄影是“艺术最致命的敌人”，是缺乏艺术天赋和训练的“所有失败画家的避难所”。如果他在 1859 年的说法可信，那么摄影就不是艺术。但今天，人们普遍认为它是艺术。

sentences.en: And in all likelihood, you think it is too.Why is that?
sentences.zh: 很可能，你也这么认为。为什么呢？

sentences.en: And if you have an answer, you'd have to argue why AI generated images wouldn't follow the same trajectory.
sentences.zh: 如果你有答案，你就必须争论为什么人工智能生成的图像不会遵循相同的轨迹。

blocks.html_en:
Your quick take lacks perspective. Photography wasn't always viewed to be art. Critics called photography "slop" in its infancy for a long while. See Charles Baudelaire for his 1800's take on photography:

> As the photographic industry was the refuge of every would-be painter, every painter too ill-endowed or too lazy to complete his studies, this universal infatuation bore not only the mark of a blindness, an imbecility, but had also the air of a vengeance. I do not believe, or at least I do not wish to believe, in the absolute success of such a brutish conspiracy, in which, as in all others, one finds both fools and knaves; but I am convinced that the ill-applied developments of photography, like all other purely material developments of progress, have contrib­uted much to the impoverishment of the French artistic genius, which is already so scarce.

Harsh. It wasn't a fringe view either. I encourage you to read how much creatives despised photography.

This argument was transferred to film when it first came out as well. It took a long while and a couple court cases before it was accepted that it took editorial choice for a photograph and film to be good. When it was accepted that to be the case, despite the aspects of mechanical reproduction, it was also accepted into the pantheon of fine art.

So it will be for AI generated images and video. So far, I've seen nothing inherent in the properties of AI generated media as a medium that obviates a human editorial eye. Even if AI could exercise comparable judgement, we will like an image because we want the curation of a specific person.

In Grant Sanderson's interview with Dwarkesh Patel about the future role of mathematicians (36:25), he says:

> One interesting take that I've heard about what mathematicians will end up being is that it's actually more analogous to art museum curators than anything else. The AI solved the thing, so the art exists. They even know how to explain it really well. But you still want someone to help you navigate this nearly infinite space of what ideas are worth engaging with. Even if AIs were in some sense better at that, I think we would always still prefer a human that we had a relationship with, because the way we get motivated to be interested in things is a social phenomenon. If you have some specific technology you're trying to build, that might be different. But the people listening to this podcast trust your curation on what's an interesting topic in the first place. It's not that they're landing here because whatever your next topic is, that's what they wanted to understand in a prior sense. They're trusting you as a curator. So my role, and arguably that of other mathematicians, might actually just shift subtly into that curation direction of what ideas are worth pursuing. That's a lot of my job right now.

Hence, I think there will be a role for AI generated images and video to be elevated into the fine art in the next couple of decades, and we'll see them in museums and exhibitions--as well more mundane uses like what's sitting on your phone right now--just like how photographs are used today.

"Self‐Portrait as a Drowned Man" is thought to be the first staged photograph and it carries a powerful artistic and political message.

Literally everyone in the world with access to a browser can prompt chatgpt for an image. Billions of AI images have been generated yet you can't point literally to a single one.

Illiterate hunter gatherers in the Paleolithic with a life expectancy of mid-20s scrounged what few pigments they could muster and left their hands' imprints on stone. Even in this age of globalization, immediate access to information, and the sum of human knowledge on your pocket, having stood in one of these caves I can tell you it's breathtaking. But once we have AGI and ASI the Minds will produce great art! Super related to current transformer architecture slop.

blocks.html_en:
Was "Self‐Portrait as a Drowned Man" thought of as great art at the time it was taken in 1840? Or was its status as great art a retroactive judgement with the perspective of time by people after 1840?

Not being familiar with the piece, so I looked it up. Seems like it was a protest correspondence aimed at a specific institution, not a public artwork. It doesn't appear to have been exhibited, reviewed, or discussed in print in 1840. Mostly circulated privately.

So I don't think it's a good test. Because you're asking me to point out an equivalent piece in the billions of generative art produced in these six years that would be judged by future historians to have great artistic value. If we were both back in 1840, we both wouldn't be able to point out "Self‐Portrait as a Drowned Man" either. It never posed itself as art at the time, and we'd have to know what future art historians thought.

Yes, I stand by the "lacking perspective" comment, because your judgements on photography and what's considered art are from the current modern point of view, rather than putting yourself in the shoes of those judging photography when it first came out--which is the shoes we find ourselves wearing when it comes to judging generative images, because the alternative (retrospectively judging it from the future) is unavailable to us.

Hence, my core argument still stands. In what way is photography different than generated images, where in photography is considered art because humans can exercise their creative judgement, but in generative images isn't because humans cannot exercise their creative judgement?

To argue against my own stance, the tact you should have taken could have been:

If one major component of art is the human judgement, how could humans could be credited for exercising any judgement at all when prompting, when LLMs are at the end of the pipe? And if they're at all intelligence, what's to say they're not superseding our intentions with their own?

blocks.html_en:
Okay but that’s exactly what the painters said about photography when it was invented. They said it was more chemistry than art because of the development process.

  Photography couldn’t qualify as an art in its own right, the explanation went, because it lacked “something beyond mere mechanism at the bottom of it.

https://daily.jstor.org/when-photography-was-not-art/

I don’t see how blanket labeling all images made with AI as slop is any different from people rejecting photographs because they were made with chemicals and lenses.

In 100 years the same article will be written about AI art, and will probably feature the phrase “clanker slop”.

  Le Havre, he called it Impression. The term, springing from the jargon used by painters, had been an artistic watchword since the middle of the century, reflecting the growing interest in capturing the atmosphere of a scene, or impression, rather than giving a painstaking description of nature

So give the above it's really futile to debate over whether any particular image is art. But yeah, drop a contact if you want recs!

Yeah exactly, I think the massive volume increase in content requires more aggressively filtering what you pay attention to. My tolerance for bad content has gone to nothing because the second I realize I can prompt the same article into existence except more personalized, I’m out - and the next time I see that company/person’s blog, I’m ignoring it.

Not everything made with some kind of AI assistance is slop, but all slop is made by AI.

blocks.html_en:
I find images are good for speed-reading; they convey information that otherwise would require much more time-consuming attention. I'm significantly more likely to read a long article, after skimming it, if it contains contextual images.

Personally, I'm okay with AI generated images as long as it's not obvious or slop: For me, a carefully-prompted image is on par with a carefully chosen photo, carefully chosen diagram, ect.

I also hold blog entries to a lower standard than professional content: I'm much more likely (after skimming) to read an imperfect non-professional blog entry than (after skimming) imperfect professional content. (And professional content is where I expect images that are higher quality than AI prompting.)

sentences.en: I find images are good for speed-reading; they convey information that otherwise would require much more time-consuming attention.
sentences.zh: 我发现图像有助于快速阅读；它们传达的信息原本需要花费更多时间来关注。

sentences.zh: 如果一篇长文章包含上下文图像，我在浏览后更有可能阅读它。就我个人而言，我对人工智能生成的图像没问题，只要它不明显或不明显：对我来说，精心提示的图像与精心挑选的照片、精心选择的图表等相当。我对博客条目的标准也低于专业内容：我更有可能（浏览后）阅读不完美的非专业博客条目，而不是（浏览后）略读）专业内容不完善。

sentences.en: (And professional content is where I expect images that are higher quality than AI prompting.)
sentences.zh: （专业内容是我期望图像质量比人工智能提示更高的地方。）

blocks.html_en: In traditional publishing publishers view the cover as a marketing tool - Arthur C Clark had negligible influence over what appeared on the covers of his books in his career when 2001 was released. That's not self-expression by any definition. You could hire a human to do art for you if you like, that's also not self-expression, nor is using an AI to do art for you. There's no meaningful self-expression in the act of having other people make things for you, they're doing the expression, you're enjoying (or not enjoying) the result.

It just makes me wonder what else in your content is AI-generated. Just sows a little seed of distrust.

People did it before and they do it now. Everybody doesn't do it, but it's not true that "nobody" does it. That could be part of why people's brains are honing in on it as a heuristic.

blocks.html_en:
For me the breaking point for images in texts was stock photos.

Before that, when there was a photo in the article it was a frame from a footage from the event or the photo, or the schematic of the device the article was about or something. Something relevant to that particular piece of information.

But then everything became click-bait factory illustrated by images that fit the mood.

AI images don't make it worse. Don't make it better. But they might if they get better at relevant infographics. For now they aren't good enough because they rely on a human for understanding of what are they to depic and humans often don't care enough.

blocks.html_en:
If you use images on your blog, even if you are scrupulous about sourcing them, purchase licenses, or go by the same low-resolution "fair use" rules that Wikipedia does, you will get several letters a year from law firms claiming they represent a client who owns the right to that photo.

Rather than wasting time sorting all these out when the images are there mostly to break up a wall of text, some blogs simply use a few AI images. This way if those letters come, they can simply put them in the bin.

I don't object to this use of AI images at all.

Then the author said:

> I know there are plenty of things you can roast my blog for but at least you know for a fact you’re getting the thoughts of a real human being and not some LLM.

So it is OK for you to use AI generation tools like Claude Code and likely using it in your blog or using it to generate code, but it isn't OK for you to see someone else using AI to generate images?

Why preach fake principles with virtue signalling and then break your own standards in your own blog post?

blocks.html_en:
I find them very interesting and they make me more likely to remember your blog. I was reading that Gas Town post yesterday and despite all the backlash about the whimsical world and the ai images being sloppy and wrong, they still stuck in my brain more than anything else I’ve read this year.

The author say they’d prefer Microsoft paint images but actually I don’t think this is true of most audiences. People have the ability to make terrible paint images for decades and they’ve never caught anyone’s attention in a positive way, it’s not going to start now.

OP’s blog of white text on black background will be forgotten quickly. If I visit it again, I will have no recollection of ever having visited. I’m not saying they need to use AI, but to oppose AI with the opposite —- minimal design or even intentionally crappy design — will not have the intended effect of communicating “this is quality human-authored content”, it will just be forgettable.

blocks.html_en:
On the other hand, plenty of art can lean into being intentionally brash and be all the more memorable for it. The phrase "bad MS paint blog" immediately makes me think of Hyperbole and a Half[1] where the style feeds into the zany ADHD vibe of the blog.

Often, you find ugliness and rule breaking as a backlash to an overly polished status quo. AM radio rock gave way to punk, hair metal gave way to grunge, and EDM gave way to hyperpop. The most iconic album cover of 2024 was the word "brat" badly rendered on a plain, garish background.[2]

[1] https://hyperboleandahalf.blogspot.com/2010/05/sneaky-hate-s...

[2] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brat_(album)

blocks.html_en: On the other hand, plenty of art can lean into being intentionally brash and be all the more memorable for it. The phrase "bad MS paint blog" immediately makes me think of Hyperbole and a Half[1] where the style feeds into the zany ADHD vibe of the blog.

sentences.zh: 另一方面，很多艺术都可以故意表现得傲慢，并因此而更加令人难忘。

sentences.en: The phrase "bad MS paint blog" immediately makes me think of Hyperbole and a Half[1] where the style feeds into the zany ADHD vibe of the blog.
sentences.zh: “糟糕的 MS 绘画博客”这个短语立即让我想起夸张和一半[1]，其中的风格融入了博客滑稽的多动症氛围。

blocks.html_en: Often, you find ugliness and rule breaking as a backlash to an overly polished status quo. AM radio rock gave way to punk, hair metal gave way to grunge, and EDM gave way to hyperpop. The most iconic album cover of 2024 was the word "brat" badly rendered on a plain, garish background.[2]

blocks.html_en:
> People have the ability to make terrible paint images for decades and they’ve never caught anyone’s attention in a positive way

Citation needed for this one. It could be because people don't do it very much? I think a very good piece of writing coupled with a crappy but intentional MS Paint piece could be very attention catching and memorable.

> OP’s blog of white text on black background will be forgotten quickly.

I actually get annoyed with the tech crowd always complaining at seemingly the slightest bit of flair or fun added to any blog. To each their own, of course. I've seen some really slick minimal blogs but I do like it when layouts gets creative--gawdy, even!--, so long as I can read the text. And you can always use reader mode.

blocks.html_en:
Barely longer than a Tweet. Low effort slop. /half sarcasm.

I record 20-40 minutes of "uneditied, one take no fake" Podcast/Vlog per day and have been using AI to generate the cover image + video description and sometimes title for YouTube lately. Also somewhat low effort, I admit. I have project ideas to upcycle the raw takes. (iSpooge Daily on YouTube, support links on channel page).

My likes and views are consistently up since using Gen AI for said tasks. It's extremely niche, just yapping about existence and ideas as a homeless unemployed software engineer in Christ on daily walks. Some of the most authentic stuff online, in my opinion, criminally underrated. The AI art covers and generated metadata are better than I could do even given unlimited time + resources.

content_html_zh: 对我来说，包含图像有不同的动机，其中一些对于人工智能生成来说是很好的。 如果图像实际上有助于说明或解释实际内容，那么根据它的生成方式来拒绝它似乎是非常肤浅的。 事实上，坚持某人盲目地手绘一些本来可以用更简单的方法完成的东西是有点愚蠢的。当图像被放置为错误的价值信号时，问题就出现了。 如果它的目的是发出这样的信号：“这个内容花了很多精力来制作，因为上面附加了人类很难制作的图像”——但图像是在没有付出这种努力的情况下生成的，那么它基本上是对读者的谎言和侮辱。就像天花板上的聚苯乙烯泡沫塑料灰泥一样。装饰和装饰品总是表明对某些事物付出了额外的努力，表明它被制造商/所有者认为是重要的和重视的。 但人们也有动机进行更便宜的模仿。 然后观众就有动力去区分真假，看看真正的、稀缺的努力去了哪里。 这些动态对于理解人工智能周围的感受和情绪至关重要。 价值几乎从来不在于事物本身或某些内在品质，而在于社会信号和关系。 （对于非常实用的工程机械或维持生计水平的基本必需品来说，情况有些不太正确）。在博客中，真实图像意味着您花了很多时间来创建帖子，这对您来说非常重要，并且您可能确保文本中的细节是准确的。而博客中的 AI 图像意味着轻松大量发布，其中文本可能只是从 AI 中复制而无需任何注意。文章作者应该更仔细地指定哪种类型的图像。 库存图片网站已经使通用照片和图画的价格变得便宜。 事实上，它们看起来很便宜。 喷漆越多、质量越高，它看起来就越便宜。 如果牙医网站上有廉价的美丽护士照片，那么它的价值就低于摄影师在其所在地拍摄的真实照片。很难清楚地表达这些东西，特别是很难向我们中间迷恋的人工智能解释它，因为他们并不真正想理解为什么人们不喜欢他们所痴迷的工具。 人工智能擅长很多事情，消化大量信息，其中大部分是代码。 对我来说，其他一切看起来/听起来都像狗屎。 人工智能音乐听起来沉闷且制作过度，就像许多中等流行音乐一样。 人工智能图像看起来过度调整和奇怪，就像杂志编辑一样，如果他们对工具没有自我控制的话。 它只是... 看起来很糟糕。 作为一种审美。 如果你没有审美意识，你可能不会在意，或者你可能无法分辨，那也没关系。 但我是，而且我可以，如果我打开你的博客文章并看到人工智能垃圾，我就会离开。 我不会要求其他人这样做，如果我世界上最好的朋友想在你的人工智能生成的日落中击败他的肉，我也不在乎，这对他有好处，我希望他玩得很开心。 但我不感兴趣。我很奇怪为什么这些超级支持人工智能的人会认为这是对个人的蔑视。 你并没有足够关心去真正制作一些东西，如果我告诉你我真的不想看它，你有什么生气吗？这些工具正在变得越来越好，而且通常过度生产的东西就是假发效果，你不会注意到更好的工具。 通过更多定制的提示可以避免通用的外观。 即使您不会唱歌，您也可以通过更长的提示、添加一些快速自唱的旋律作为参考来制作更自然的歌曲。 同样，对于图像来说，在油漆中勾勒出一些东西可以产生巨大的差异，或者只是迭代 2 或 3 次而不接受第一个结果。而且工具也会变得更好。> 特别难以向我们当中迷恋的人工智能解释这一点，因为他们并不真正想理解为什么人们不喜欢他们所痴迷的工具。您的评论是家长评论正在讨论的一个例子；反射性的“你真的不能说出来，无论如何你可以做得更好，阻止人们能够说出来，而且很快就会变得更好，所以没有人能够说出来”是一种像自恋者的祈祷一样的奔腾。人们告诉你他们可以说出来，而且他们确实在乎。 假发谬论之所以有效，是因为有些好的假发除非被告知，否则没有人能够识别，但认为实际上存在出色的人工智能散文（没有人发现）的想法总是缺乏例子。关心人的因素和人际关系是很好的。 类比：想要手里拿着一张大黑胶唱片，看看艺术品，用指尖抚摸唱片套，闻一闻唱片的气味并享受这种体验，这很好。 只是，正如“数字CD音乐是量化的，听起来比模拟音乐差”被揭露为无稽之谈一样，“我能看出它是人工智能，所以我不喜欢它”也经不起时间的考验。 你仍然可以出于人类的原因想要人类的音乐，但你将无法区分它们。尽管“AI Slop”很简单，但它似乎被误解了：“这是草率/省力/不熟练的工作...... ”。>“人们告诉你他们可以告诉你，而且他们确实关心。”本着同样的精神，人们可能会说“AI Slop”实际上是一种小程度的建设性反馈。 这是“这是一项草率/省力/不熟练的工作，明显利用了生成式人工智能工具”的简写。 这与在 Instagram 上为每个帖子使用相同的摄影滤镜或选择最受欢迎的 Wordpress 主题没有太大区别——如果您期待对此的赞扬，那么您会感到失望。我确实非常喜欢这一点，显然在阿尔法一代中，当有人说一些非常愚蠢的事情，或者制造出质量很差的东西时，人们会说它是“人工智能”，这是很常见的事情。孩子们都很好。最大的错误是认为你的审美观是“正确的”。当你拥护你的审美偏好是普遍的时候，你就对自己进行了个人的蔑视，然后进一步中伤具有不同偏好的人，说他们没有审美意识。是的，是的，当然，没有什么审美偏好是坏的。
